verses.text: Yahweh said to Samuel, “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite; for I have provided a king for myself among his sons.”
Samuel said, “How can I go? If Saul hears it, he will kill me.” Yahweh said, “Take a heifer with you, and say, I have come to sacrifice to Yahweh.
Call Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you shall do. You shall anoint to me him whom I name to you.”
Samuel did that which Yahweh spoke, and came to Bethlehem. The elders of the city came to meet him trembling, and said, “Do you come peaceably?”
He said, “Peaceably; I have come to sacrifice to Yahweh. Sanctify yourselves, and come with me to the sacrifice.” He sanctified Jesse and his sons, and called them to the sacrifice.
When they had come, he looked at Eliab, and said, “Surely Yahweh’s anointed is before him.”

But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
Then Jesse called Abinadab, and made him pass before Samuel. He said, “Yahweh has not chosen this one, either.”
Then Jesse made Shammah to pass by. He said, “Yahweh has not chosen this one, either.”
Jesse made seven of his sons to pass before Samuel. Samuel said to Jesse, “Yahweh has not chosen these.”

Samuel said to Jesse, “Are all your children here?” He said, “There remains yet the youngest. Behold, he is keeping the sheep.” Samuel said to Jesse, “Send and get him, for we will not sit down until he comes here.”
He sent, and brought him in. Now he was ruddy, with a handsome face and good appearance. Yahweh said, “Arise! Anoint him, for this is he.”
Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the middle of his brothers. Then Yahweh’s Spirit came mightily on David from that day forward. So Samuel rose up and went to Ramah.
Now Yahweh’s Spirit departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from Yahweh troubled him.
Saul’s servants said to him, “See now, an evil spirit from God troubles you.

Let our lord now command your servants who are in front of you to seek out a man who is a skillful player on the harp. Then when the evil spirit from God is on you, he will play with his hand, and you will be well.”
Saul said to his servants, “Provide me now a man who can play well, and bring him to me.”

Then one of the young men answered, and said, “Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite who is skillful in playing, a mighty man of valor, a man of war, prudent in speech, and a handsome person; and Yahweh is with him.”
Therefore Saul sent messengers to Jesse, and said, “Send me David your son, who is with the sheep.”
Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, and a bottle of wine, and a young goat, and sent them by David his son to Saul.
David came to Saul, and stood before him. He loved him greatly; and he became his armor bearer.
Saul sent to Jesse, saying, “Please let David stand before me; for he has found favor in my sight.”
When the spirit from God was on Saul, David took the harp, and played with his hand; so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him.

footnotes.content: The Lord knows how to end one chapter and begin another. Samuel was still grieving Saul's kingship when Yahweh said: Look forward. I have already chosen the one I want. How often do we tarry in yesterday's sorrows while the Lord stands ready to show us His next purpose?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samuel's fear was real—Saul would kill him if word got out. But he voiced it aloud to the Lord. And the Lord answered: Yes, go, but carry a cover, a sacrifice. He does not dismiss our fears; He walks through them with us, giving us both courage and wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh's word to Samuel was specific: I will show you. Invite Jesse to the feast, and when you see the one I name, anoint him. The Lord does not ask us to guess or second-guess. He makes His choice plain when we are faithful to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the elders of Bethlehem trembled at Samuel's arrival. An old prophet showing up unannounced in a small town? Their fear shows how much the times had weighed on Israel. But Samuel came in peace—and peace from a messenger of Yahweh carries its own quiet authority.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samuel sanctified Jesse and his sons—that ancient ritual of separation, of making holy space. When we set apart time to seek the Lord's will, we prepare ourselves to hear it. The ordinary sacrifice becomes the threshold where the Divine steps in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliab walked in first, and Samuel's eye caught him—tall, strong, a man who looked the part of a king. How quickly we assume the outside tells the whole story. Samuel was ready to make the same mistake we all make.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't look on his face or stature—I don't see as man sees. The Lord sees the heart. This word, spoken at the moment Samuel was about to err, is a rebuke and a gift. It teaches us that all our human measuring—appearance, credentials, strength—misses the thing that matters most to God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abinadab passed before Samuel, and the word came again: not this one. How many times in this chapter does Yahweh say no? Each refusal is a mercy, keeping Samuel patient, keeping him listening. The Lord is teaching His prophet to wait for clarity, not to settle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shammah passed, and again: not this one either. Three sons in, and Samuel has heard nothing but no. But notice—he does not doubt. He does not demand explanations. He simply watches, and listens, and lets the Lord's will unfold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All seven sons—a full number, the number of completeness—passed before Samuel. Yet none was the one. How patient Yahweh is to say no seven times, guiding His servant's eye toward the truth He has already chosen but Samuel has not yet seen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Are all your children here? The question that changes everything. The youngest was out in the fields with the sheep—not grand enough to invite to a prophet's visit, not valued enough to be counted among the sons. Yet he was the one Yahweh had chosen. The last shall be first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He was ruddy, with a handsome face and good appearance. David was beautiful to look upon, yet the Lord did not choose him for his face—He saw the heart beneath. We learn too late, and too often, that beauty and worth are not the same. But the Lord knew it from the start.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the middle of his brothers, Samuel anointed him. David was anointed in their presence, set apart among them—not in secret, not in shame, but openly before his kin. The oil poured out, the Spirit came mightily, and everything changed in that small house in Bethlehem.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Spirit of Yahweh departed from Saul. In the same hour the Spirit came mightily on David, Saul began to be troubled. The old king's hold was loosening. The new king's kingship was beginning. The transition, though hidden, had begun.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The servants saw it plainly—an evil spirit troubles you. Saul's own household recognized that something had broken in him. Sometimes those closest to us see our decline before we name it ourselves. Saul was beginning a long, dark unraveling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They suggested: let us find a skillful harp player. When the evil spirit comes on you, he will play, and you will be well. Even the servants believed that music, that ancient language of the soul, could soothe what ailed the king. And they were not wrong.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul said: Find me a man who plays well. He commanded, and the machinery of search began to turn. No one knew that the Lord had already provided the answer—the youngest son of Jesse, sleeping in the fields with sheep, about to be summoned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One of the young men answered: I have seen a son of Jesse—skillful in playing, a mighty man of valor, a man of war, prudent in speech, handsome, and Yahweh is with him. This description is so full, so specific—it is not casual praise but a recognition that the Lord's favor rests on David.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul sent messengers to Jesse: Send me David your son, who is with the sheep. The king of Israel commanded that a shepherd boy be brought before him. David would have had no idea what awaited him, no warning of how his life was about to become entwined with Saul's, forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jesse sent David with a gift—bread, wine, and a kid. A father's careful provision: go to the king with something to offer. Small gifts, humble gifts, carried by a young man from Bethlehem toward a destiny he could not have imagined.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul loved him greatly and he became his armor bearer. That was quick—from the fields to the king's side in one visit. The connection between them was immediate, almost inexplicable. How often does the Lord open doors so suddenly that our breath catches?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul sent word: Let David stand before me; he has found favor in my sight. The favor that matters always comes from the Lord, yet it flows through human hearts. David had found favor first in Yahweh's eyes, and now in Saul's. The thread of Providence was weaving tight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the spirit from God was on Saul, David took the harp and played, and Saul was refreshed and well. Readers today hear an echo in this simple gift of music—how often the Lord soothes our troubled hearts through beauty, through art, through the gifts of those He has placed near us. What we do with hands and heart, done in faith, can be a balm to others' suffering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
